This is The Memo by Howard Marks.
Today, we're featuring another episode of The Rewind,
in which Howard looks back on some of his memos over the years,
discusses their origin, and considers their relevance to today's financial environment.
Today, Howard reflects on bubble.com,
which was originally published on January 2, 2000.
Here's Howard.
We had all been living with the tech and internet stock rise
for years at this point, you know, and probably the last five years of the 90s.
It was in 96 that Alan Greenspan said, are we beginning to see signs of irrational exuberance?
It reached its apogee in 99, you know.
I remember I was on the Penn Investment Committee, and one of the schools, I think,
had a return of 40% in its endowment that year, and its venture capital investments were up
250%. So the growth stock outperformance that year was probably the greatest
that's ever been, maybe until this year. So I started to think about it, but what really moved me was when
I read this book, The Devil Take the Hindmost, which I identify in the first line here, it was a
chronicle of financial speculation. The South Sea bubble was one of the greatest of those.
I mentioned in the last podcast that I see parallels and analogies, and that's what this was.
You read that at the time, and as shown on the bottom of page one and the top page two,
there are all these similarities between what had been seen in the South Sea bubble 300 years earlier
and what was going on in the tech bubble.
And that really got me going.
Now, I had to learn a lot because I'm not a technologist, so I probably worked on this for three
months and then probably finished my work over the Christmas vacation and was able to get
it out on the first business day of 2000.
And what I like to say is that I, after 10 years, I became an overnight success with the memos.
The response to the memo itself was very positive. I think the memo was well argued. But the other thing is
that it was right and it was right quickly. You know, if you're right slowly, it doesn't help.
But it was right within a few months because there's an old saying in our business that being too

far ahead of its time. Other people who had blown the whistle in 96 or 97 or 98, they were
too far ahead of their time. And, you know, they suffered for it. It lost money from their management.
Now, this does not relate to our management because we're in the credit markets and technology

companies are too risky to borrow any money. So this was not in our commercial wheelhouse,
but it was something worth observing.
What actually started me on the memo was reading the chancellor book, Devil Take the Highmost,
and seeing commonalities between the historic behavior described in the book and the actual behavior
that was taking place in real time before my eyes.

the idea of people investing heavily in things.
they didn't understand and investing in things that they couldn't value.

is as a lottery ticket. In this instance, in particular, there were
a lot of lottery tickets. Some of them turned out to be very valuable. But what

was very poor, and people were giving up on stocks. So there's the cycle that when they do well,

going to do poorly forever. Now, the reverse is more true. When they do well, it sets the scene for them
them to do poorly. And when they do poorly, it sets the scene for them to do well. But most people extrapolate
rather than understand concepts like regression to the mean. Most people think that
When stocks go up, it's unmitigated good news.

I think, obviously, the outperformance of the thing, whatever it is. I think, I think,
Obviously, the outperformance of the tech stocks this year and the software stocks is one

from the TMT bubble, the internet bubble, the e-tail, and so forth.

inappropriate optimism. I'm not saying that optimism with regard to the great tech companies

which sell on the basis of what their future is. You can't have those soaring without
a component of optimism. And what is a bubble, but a rational excessive optimism.
unjustified optimism. And of course, these are, by definition, companies that can't

Conceptual investing based on optimism when taken to excess is the raw material of the bubble.

In exchange for performance, for performance,

Early in this rise, however, Newton realized the speculative nature of the boom and sold his

By September,

Despite their lack of profits, companies like South Sea were able to finance their operations

that airplanes and automobiles had been expected to change the world, and did
